Work ONLY inside /opt/nxeon-wt-admin-cleanup (a pre-created git worktree, branch `feature/coldemail-admin-cleanup`, off the Nxeon hosting platform's main repo). Do NOT touch /opt/nxeon or any other /opt/nxeon-wt-* directory — other work is happening concurrently on the same underlying cold-email system (a backend-completion effort and a lead-research effort), so stay focused on the admin UI/UX layer and avoid rewriting backend logic in `lib/coldemail/*.ts` or the Prisma schema. `node_modules` and `.env` in your worktree are symlinks to the main repo (normal) — but NEVER run `git add -A`, it's a known hazard that can corrupt the main repo's real `node_modules` through the symlink. Only ever `git add` the exact file paths you changed.

This is a real production hosting business (Next.js/TypeScript/Prisma/Postgres, Nxeon navy/violet/cyan admin theme). The owner's own words: "i feel like the cold email section is a bit cluttered, clean it up. improvise and improve."

## What you're working with

`app/admin/coldemail/` currently has 14 top-level subsections: `analytics`, `brands`, `businesses`, `campaigns`, `contacts`, `domains`, `import`, `inbox`, `lists`, `settings`, `suppression`, `templates`, `warming`, `webhooks` — plus `page.tsx` and a `components/admin/coldemail/` folder (`Controls.tsx`, `DnsVerify.tsx`, `Inbox.tsx`, `Phase3Controls.tsx`, `Webhooks.tsx`). 4,624 lines total, all built in a single day (2026-08-11), which is almost certainly why the information architecture is rough — it reads like a feature-by-feature build log rather than something designed for how an operator would actually use it day to day.

## Your job

1. **Read every page/component first** before changing anything — understand what each of the 14 sections actually does, what data it shows, and what actions it exposes. Don't guess from names alone.
2. **Diagnose the actual clutter** — likely candidates worth checking: overlapping concerns (e.g. does `brands` overlap with `domains`/`settings`? does `contacts` overlap with `businesses`/`lists`?), too many top-level nav items for what should be a handful of real workflows (list management, campaign management, deliverability/health monitoring, compliance/suppression, configuration), inconsistent patterns between sections (one might be a nice table+filters, another a wall of raw JSON), and whether the navigation groups things the way an operator actually thinks about the work (e.g. "I want to see how my campaigns are doing" vs. "I want to manage my sending domains' health") rather than the way the code happened to get built.
3. **Redesign the information architecture** — consolidate where it makes sense (e.g. maybe `brands` + `domains` + `settings` collapse into one "Sending identity" section with tabs; maybe `warming` + `webhooks` + `analytics` collapse into one "Deliverability" section) — use your judgment, but the goal is fewer, more coherent top-level destinations, not just fewer files. Every existing capability needs to still be reachable — this is about better organization, not feature removal.
4. **Match the existing Nxeon admin design language** — look at other well-established admin sections (e.g. `app/admin/free-minecraft/`, `app/admin/board/`, or the Compute Nodes page) for the actual visual conventions (spacing, card/panel patterns, semantic color use for status, table styling) already in use elsewhere in this admin panel, and make the cold-email section consistent with those rather than inventing a new visual language.
5. Since a concurrent effort is finishing the cold-email SEND pipeline and adding tracking/analytics data, and another is doing lead research, expect that the data/analytics THIS UI displays may currently be sparse or a little stale (no live campaigns running yet) — design for what the UI should look like once real data flows through it, not just for today's empty state. Make sure empty states are handled gracefully and don't look broken.

## Constraints — important

- Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npm run build` inside `/opt/nxeon-wt-admin-cleanup` before finishing.
- Manually exercise the redesigned admin pages if you can (this app has a dev server / the ability to run `npm run dev` — check for an existing convention for how other work in this session verified UI changes, e.g. via a headless browser check, if that's feasible in your environment) to confirm nothing is visually broken or missing before calling it done. If you can't get a live render, at minimum trace through the code carefully for correctness.
- Commit with a clear message describing the before/after information architecture (what moved where and why). Do NOT merge to main, do NOT touch staging, do NOT run deploy/promote scripts — a human handles integration and production deployment separately.
- Report back: the old vs. new section structure (a short list is fine), what you consolidated and why, what you deliberately left alone and why, files touched, and confirm you committed on `feature/coldemail-admin-cleanup`.

Cold Email breaks this pattern by cramming 14 tabs into a single entry, which is exactly the clutter problem — the fix is to split that one entry into several smaller ones matching the established structure.

I'm sketching a concrete redesign: convert Cold Email from one flat entry into a group with sub-entries like Leads, Sending Identity, Campaigns, Deliverability, Inbox, Compliance, and Settings — grouping related tabs (brands/domains/settings, warming/webhooks/analytics, etc.) so each entry has a coherent, manageable set of tabs mirroring the Fleet group's design.

That's still ten top-nav entries, which feels like a lot, but nesting them as tabs under fewer group entries following the admin-groups.ts pattern could work well. I'm sketching out "Cold Email" as a group with entries like Overview, Leads (Businesses/Lists/Import), Campaigns (Campaigns/Templates), Inbox, and Sending identity (Brands/Domains/Warming/Settings), though I need to reconcile where warming actually belongs.

Deliverability could pull in Analytics, Warming, and Webhooks, while Compliance covers Suppression -- that's seven entries under one Cold Email group, roughly in line with how Fleet and Revenue are structured. But looking closer, Cold Email currently sits as a single 14-tab entry inside the Marketing group alongside Marketing and Studio, so the cleanest fix is probably to keep Cold Email as one entry rather than splitting it into its own group.
